extracted.intended_audience: researchers and journal editors interested in peer review incentives (scientometrics scholars, editorial boards)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and analysing a natural experiment to test whether non-monetary rewards (e.g., publishing reviewer names, reviewer certificates) affect willingness to become peer reviewers; includes measurement, hypotheses, and statistical modelling guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward contingencies (engagement-contingent, task-completion-contingent, performance-contingent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three categories of reward contingencies are identified and defined: engagement-contingent (given for mere agreement to be involved), completion-contingent (given for completing the task), and performance-contingent (given for high performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and expected motivational effects are given using Cognitive Evaluation Theory: engagement conveys little control or competence signal and likely small effects; completion is perceived as controlling but conveys no quality signal and likely little impact; performance conveys a strong signal of effort/competence but also a strong controlling effect that can reduce intrinsic motivation. The paper treats these as the primary experimental manipulanda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-monetary reward: publishing reviewers' names and issuing reviewer certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific non-monetary reward tested is acknowledgement by publishing reviewers' names on the journal’s website and issuing a reviewer certificate upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'ribbon' type reward is motivated as commonly used by journals and hypothesized to provide reputational payoff without monetary drawbacks. It is the operationalized incentive across the experimental conditions (visible after opening the email).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivational categories for peer review (intrinsic, prosocial, extrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists' motivations are classified as enjoyment/intrinsic, service to the academic community/prosocial, and extrinsic motives (e.g., career advancement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature review and theory emphasize intrinsic and prosocial motivations as primary drivers of peer reviewing; extrinsic motivations are generally weaker. Theoretical implications (e.g., crowding out of intrinsic motivation by external rewards) are used to predict effects of incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent measure: Email opened as proxy for general interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the contacted person opened the invitation email (measured the same day) is used as a first dependent variable and proxy for general interest in becoming a reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement relies on MailChimp tracking of 'opens'. The experimental setting was only visible after opening, so opening is treated separately from acceptance and used to define the analytic sample for the acceptance models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent measure: Acceptance to become reviewer (same-day binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the contacted person accepted to become a reviewer within the first day after receiving the invitation (coded 1 for accept, 0 for not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-day window is imposed to minimize contamination across experimental arms; acceptance within the same day is used to avoid cross-awareness. Analyses of acceptance are run on those who opened the email the same day (sample selection acknowledged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort/provision measures: number of manuscripts and time availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents who accepted were asked how many articles they were available to review each year and how many months they foresaw to provide a review report; these are used as measures of intended effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive comparisons across experimental groups examine whether contingencies change promised effort (e.g., performance setting respondents foresee slightly less number of manuscripts and more time per review). Differences tested with Kruskal–Wallis non-parametric tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variable: Reward setting (no-reward, engagement, completion, performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental assignment of invitees to one of four categorical reward conditions: no reward (baseline), engagement (reward for joining pool), completion (reward for completing at least one review), performance (reward conditional on quality/quantity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment aimed to produce similar proportions by faculty, university type, rank, and gender. The experimental text is visible only after opening the email, and acceptance comparisons are conditional on opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variable: Type of institutional affiliation (public vs private)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliation with public versus private university is used as a predictor and moderator (dummy variable private versus public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory expects public-university scientists to be more receptive to public acknowledgment (reward) than private-university scientists; hypothesis H4 formalizes that private-affiliated scientists will be less likely to accept under the publish-your-name reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variable: Gender (female vs male)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent gender (female versus male) is included as a predictor and interaction moderator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory and prior evidence lead to hypothesis H2 that, under performance-contingent rewards, female scientists may be more likely to accept than male peers. Descriptive and regression interaction terms (e.g., performance*female) are used to test differential responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variable: Academic rank (teaching assistant, assistant, associate, full professor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic rank is included as a categorical predictor (teaching assistant, assistant professor, associate professor, full professor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis H3 expects ranks more research-focused (associate professors) to be more likely to accept than ranks more teaching-focused (assistants, teaching assistants) or managerial (full professors). Rank differences are examined in opening and acceptance rates and regression models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variable: Scientific productivity (articles, proceedings, h-index; factor score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific productivity is measured by number of articles, number of proceeding articles, and Hirsch index; a factor analysis extracts a single productivity factor rescaled to range between 1 and 11.4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productivity is modeled as a continuous predictor and interaction moderator with experimental conditions; Hypothesis H5 predicts that high-productivity scientists will be less responsive (less likely to accept) under performance-contingent rewards. Factor analytic combination and its scaling are specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample inclusion/exclusion rules and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample construction rules: contact details from 35 universities, duplicates and inconsistent names removed, those who had published/submitted in past 5 years or were already in reviewers' pool excluded; final pool 1865 scientists (87.2% public, 57.3% female, distribution by rank specified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural constraints and exclusions are documented as part of experimental validity. The invitation was sent once (no reminders). The composition informs balancing and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment and balancing of experimental groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals were assigned to the four experimental settings aiming to obtain similar proportions by faculty, university type, academic rank, and gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing across covariates is used to support causal comparisons between reward settings given the natural experiment context. Small differences in opening rates across groups are attributed to chance because experimental condition text was only visible after opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule to avoid contamination: same-day opening and acceptance only
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses consider only scientists who opened and accepted within the first day to reduce the risk that respondents learned about other experimental settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to preserve the validity of the assignment and avoid cross-arm awareness; the authors report checks comparing same-day versus all acceptances to ensure performance effects persist beyond timing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of logistic regression for binary outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because dependent variables (open email; accept to be reviewer) are binary, logistic regression models are employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models include fixed effects for predictors and multilevel structure for nesting. Descriptive followed by inferential statistics are used; odds ratios computed via exp(coefficient). Alternative approaches (Heckman) were considered for selection but did not converge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistic regression assumptions and diagnostic tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Four key logistic regression assumptions are listed and checked: independence of observations, absence of multicollinearity, adequate sample size (rule-of-thumb), and linearity of continuous predictors with log odds (Box-Tidwell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence handled via same-day restriction; multicollinearity tested via Variance Inflation Factors (VIF values reported <1.15, threshold <10); sample size rule-of-thumb applied (10 cases per IV); Box-Tidwell test used for continuous productivity variable (not significant). These diagnostics are required to justify logistic model validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-selection correction (Heckman) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A Heckman two-step correction is noted as appropriate for non-randomly selected acceptance sample (those who opened the email), but the model did not converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors explain why Heckman would be appropriate and state their decision to run two separate models (open and accept) given convergence issues and empirical checks that opening differences are minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilevel modelling for nested data and Bayesian MCMC estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists (level 1) are nested into faculties (level 2); multilevel models are used and estimated via Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) due to bias in maximum-likelihood estimates for these models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and references for multilevel/Bayesian approach are provided. Starting estimates derived from maximum likelihood followed by MCMC; DIC used as diagnostic for model comparison in Bayesian context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model comparison and fit measures (DIC, AIC, sensitivity, specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For model comparison and assessing goodness-of-fit, the paper uses Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) for Bayesian models, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) for model selection, and computes predicted probabilities to evaluate classification performance via sensitivity and specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower DIC/AIC indicates better model (penalizes complexity). Predicted probabilities are thresholded to compute sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate); multiple thresholds are examined to assess fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis H1: Performance-contingent reward reduces willingness to accept vs no-reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis 1 states that scientists subjected to a performance-contingent reward are less likely to accept to become reviewers than scientists in a no-reward setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding reported: the performance contingency strongly reduces the number of respondents willing to become reviewers (−60% compared to a no-reward setting) and shows lower acceptance rates in descriptive tables and regression coefficients (performance versus baseline negative effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis H2: Under performance-contingent reward, female scientists more likely to accept than males
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis 2 predicts that under a performance-contingent reward setting, female scientists are more likely to accept to become reviewers than their male peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prior evidence on gender responsiveness to awards and recognition; regression interaction (performance*female) tested and reported significant in some specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis H3: Research-focused ranks (associate profs) more likely to accept than teaching/managerial ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis 3 predicts that academic ranks more focused on research (associate professors) are more likely to accept becoming reviewers than ranks focused on teaching (assistant professors, teaching assistants) and managerial tasks (full professors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale provided regarding role-specific incentives and time constraints; descriptive statistics and regression contrasts (associate vs full professor) are used to test the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis H4: Publishing reviewer names discourages private-university scientists relative to public
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis 4 predicts that under a reward consisting in publishing reviewers' names, scientists affiliated with private universities are less likely to accept to become reviewers than peers at public universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory: public institutions align with prosocial recognition more than private institutions whose goals emphasize profit/teaching; interactions (exp * university_type) are examined in models (completion and performance * private reported negative effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis H5: High-productivity scientists less responsive to performance-contingent rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis 5 predicts that under a performance-contingent reward setting, scientists with higher productivity will be less likely to accept to become reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: high-productivity scientists have stronger intrinsic motivations and may be discouraged by controlling performance rewards; tested via interaction between experimental condition and productivity (exp * productivity models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural measurement detail: using MailChimp to detect opens and restricting to first-day responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The operational measurement of 'email opened' relied on MailChimp tracking; acceptance is measured as same-day acceptance to reduce contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors justify using MailChimp and same-day restriction and report robustness checks comparing same-day versus all acceptances to confirm patterns (performance setting remains less effective).
